claim: TAPBPR can catalyse the dissociation of peptides from peptide-MHC I complexes in vitro.
source: We show that TAPBPR can catalyse the dissociation of peptides from peptide-MHC I complexes, enhance the loading of peptide-receptive MHC I molecules, and discriminate between peptides based on affinity in vitro.
evidence: Demonstrated through fluorescence polarization experiments showing enhanced peptide dissociation from HLA-A2 and HLA-B8 in the presence of TAPBPR (Figures 2A, 2B, 4A).

claim: TAPBPR can enhance the loading of peptide-receptive MHC I molecules in vitro.
source: We show that TAPBPR can catalyse the dissociation of peptides from peptide-MHC I complexes, enhance the loading of peptide-receptive MHC I molecules, and discriminate between peptides based on affinity in vitro.
evidence: Demonstrated through fluorescence polarization experiments showing enhanced peptide association with peptide-receptive HLA-A2 and HLA-B8 in the presence of TAPBPR (Figures 2C, 4E).

claim: TAPBPR can discriminate between peptides based on affinity in vitro.
source: We show that TAPBPR can catalyse the dissociation of peptides from peptide-MHC I complexes, enhance the loading of peptide-receptive MHC I molecules, and discriminate between peptides based on affinity in vitro.
evidence: Demonstrated through peptide competition assays showing that TAPBPR enhances selection of high affinity peptides (Figures 2D, 4H).

claim: Depletion of TAPBPR increases the diversity of peptides presented on MHC I molecules in cells.
source: In cells, the depletion of TAPBPR increased the diversity of peptides presented on MHC I molecules, suggesting that TAPBPR is involved in restricting peptide presentation.
evidence: Mass spectrometry analysis showed 1607 peptides in HeLa cells vs 2074 in HeLa-TAPBPR KO cells (Figure 5C), and similar patterns in other cell lines (Figures 5D, 6).

claim: TAPBPR is involved in restricting peptide presentation on MHC class I molecules.
source: In cells, the depletion of TAPBPR increased the diversity of peptides presented on MHC I molecules, suggesting that TAPBPR is involved in restricting peptide presentation.
evidence: Increased peptide diversity upon TAPBPR depletion and decreased diversity upon TAPBPR overexpression (Figures 5C, 5D).

claim: TAPBPR binds to MHC I in a peptide-receptive state.
source: Our results suggest TAPBPR binds to MHC I in a peptide-receptive state and, like tapasin, works to enhance peptide optimisation.
evidence: Demonstrated by peptide-induced release of MHC I from TAPBPR, with high-affinity peptide causing >90% reduction in HLA-A2 bound to TAPBPR (Figure 7).

claim: There are two MHC class I specific peptide editors, tapasin and TAPBPR, involved in controlling peptide presentation to the immune system.
source: It is now clear there are two MHC class I specific peptide editors, tapasin and TAPBPR, intimately involved in controlling peptide presentation to the immune system.
evidence: Both tapasin and TAPBPR demonstrate peptide exchange catalyst activity in vitro and affect peptide repertoire in cells.

claim: MHC class I molecules convey a selection of the peptidome of a cell to the immune system.
source: Major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I molecules convey a selection of the peptidome of a cell to the immune system.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about MHC class I function.

claim: Peptide presentation by MHC class I is relevant in the recognition of tumours.
source: As well as being of crucial importance for the detection of intracellular pathogens, particularly viruses, it is now apparent that peptide presentation by MHC class I is extremely relevant in the recognition of tumours (Rötzschke et al., 1990; Duan et al., 2014; Gubin et al., 2014; Snyder et al., 2014; Yadav et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Peptide presentation by MHC class I is crucial for the detection of intracellular pathogens, particularly viruses.
source: As well as being of crucial importance for the detection of intracellular pathogens, particularly viruses, it is now apparent that peptide presentation by MHC class I is extremely relevant in the recognition of tumours (Rötzschke et al., 1990; Duan et al., 2014; Gubin et al., 2014; Snyder et al., 2014; Yadav et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about MHC class I function.

claim: The loading of peptide onto MHC class I is orchestrated by the co-factor tapasin.
source: Currently, the loading of peptide onto MHC class I is known to be orchestrated by the co-factor tapasin and is thought to occur predominantly within the peptide loading complex (PLC) in the endoplasmic reticulum (Sadasivan et al., 1996; Li et al., 1997; Ortmann et al., 1997; Lehner et al., 1998; Tan et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Peptide loading onto MHC class I occurs predominantly within the peptide loading complex (PLC) in the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: Currently, the loading of peptide onto MHC class I is known to be orchestrated by the co-factor tapasin and is thought to occur predominantly within the peptide loading complex (PLC) in the endoplasmic reticulum (Sadasivan et al., 1996; Li et al., 1997; Ortmann et al., 1997; Lehner et al., 1998; Tan et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Tapasin enhances the rate and extent of MHC class I peptide loading.
source: Tapasin enhances the rate and the extent of MHC class I peptide loading and improves the discrimination that occurs between peptides to ensure MHC class I molecules are loaded with high-affinity peptides, thus prolonging cell surface expression of MHC class I molecules (Williams et al., 2002; Howarth et al., 2004; Chen and Bouvier, 2007; Wearsch and Cresswell, 2007; van Hateren et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Tapasin improves the discrimination between peptides to ensure MHC class I molecules are loaded with high-affinity peptides.
source: Tapasin enhances the rate and the extent of MHC class I peptide loading and improves the discrimination that occurs between peptides to ensure MHC class I molecules are loaded with high-affinity peptides, thus prolonging cell surface expression of MHC class I molecules (Williams et al., 2002; Howarth et al., 2004; Chen and Bouvier, 2007; Wearsch and Cresswell, 2007; van Hateren et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: MHC class I allomorphs differ in their dependence on tapasin for efficient peptide loading.
source: MHC class I allomorphs differ in their dependence on tapasin for efficient peptide loading (Greenwood et al., 1994;  Peh et al., 1998; Williams et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: TAPBPR is a second MHC class I-specific chaperone in addition to tapasin.
source: It has recently become apparent that, in addition to tapasin, there is a second MHC class I-specific chaperone, the tapasin-related protein TAPBPR (Boyle et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research.

claim: TAPBPR is not an integral component of the peptide loading complex.
source: In contrast to tapasin, TAPBPR is not an integral component of the peptide loading complex and cannot compensate for the loss of tapasin (Boyle et al., 2013; Hermann et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research.

claim: TAPBPR cannot compensate for the loss of tapasin.
source: In contrast to tapasin, TAPBPR is not an integral component of the peptide loading complex and cannot compensate for the loss of tapasin (Boyle et al., 2013; Hermann et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research.

claim: The presence of TAPBPR slows the anterograde trafficking of MHC class I.
source: A functional role in MHC class I antigen presentation is supported by the finding that the presence of TAPBPR slows the anterograde trafficking of MHC class I and prolongs the association of MHC class I with the PLC.
evidence: Supported by citation to published research (Boyle et al., 2013).

claim: TAPBPR prolongs the association of MHC class I with the PLC.
source: A functional role in MHC class I antigen presentation is supported by the finding that the presence of TAPBPR slows the anterograde trafficking of MHC class I and prolongs the association of MHC class I with the PLC.
evidence: Supported by citation to published research (Boyle et al., 2013).

claim: Tapasin and TAPBPR share 22% identity.
source: Although tapasin and TAPBPR only share 22% identity (Teng et al., 2002), both bind MHC class I, and their orientation on MHC class I is similar (Dong et al., 2009; Hermann et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research.

claim: Both tapasin and TAPBPR bind MHC class I.
source: Although tapasin and TAPBPR only share 22% identity (Teng et al., 2002), both bind MHC class I, and their orientation on MHC class I is similar (Dong et al., 2009; Hermann et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research.

claim: The orientation of tapasin and TAPBPR on MHC class I is similar.
source: Although tapasin and TAPBPR only share 22% identity (Teng et al., 2002), both bind MHC class I, and their orientation on MHC class I is similar (Dong et al., 2009; Hermann et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research.

claim: TAPBPR protein was efficiently produced and secreted from HEK293F cells.
source: This resulted in the efficient production of a secreted form of TAPBPR with a C-terminal His-tag, allowing for purification from the culture supernatant using Ni-affinity and size exclusion chromatography.
evidence: Demonstrated by size exclusion chromatography showing a single major peak of high purity (Figure 1A).

claim: TAPBPR protein eluted as a single major peak of high purity following size exclusion chromatography.
source: TAPBPR protein eluted as a single major peak of high purity as verified by Coomassie staining following sodium dodecyl sulfate polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1A by size exclusion chromatogram and SDS-PAGE analysis.

claim: TAPBPRTN5 (I261K mutation) was efficiently expressed and produced a major single protein peak following size-exclusion chromatography.
source: TAPBPRTN5 in which the isoleucine at position 261 was mutated to lysine, which inhibits the interaction of TAPBPR with MHC class I (Hermann et al., 2013), was produced in the same manner and was also efficiently expressed and produced a major single protein peak following size-exclusion chromatography (Figure 1B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1B by size exclusion chromatogram and SDS-PAGE analysis.

claim: The I261K mutation in TAPBPRTN5 inhibits the interaction of TAPBPR with MHC class I.
source: TAPBPRTN5 in which the isoleucine at position 261 was mutated to lysine, which inhibits the interaction of TAPBPR with MHC class I (Hermann et al., 2013), was produced in the same manner and was also efficiently expressed and produced a major single protein peak following size-exclusion chromatography (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research and confirmed by lack of functional activity in peptide dissociation assays (Figure 2B).

claim: The melting temperatures for TAPBPR and TAPBPRTN5 are between 51.5°C and 52.5°C.
source: Differential scanning fluorimetry revealed melting temperatures for TAPBPR and TAPBPRTN5 to be between 51.5°C and 52.5°C indicating that the single point mutation did not adversely affect TAPBPR folding (Figure 1C).
evidence: Measured by differential scanning fluorimetry as shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The I261K mutation did not adversely affect TAPBPR folding.
source: Differential scanning fluorimetry revealed melting temperatures for TAPBPR and TAPBPRTN5 to be between 51.5°C and 52.5°C indicating that the single point mutation did not adversely affect TAPBPR folding (Figure 1C).
evidence: Inferred from equivalent thermal denaturation profiles shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Dissociation of FLPSDC*FPSV from HLA-A2 was only apparent in the first six hours in the presence of competitor peptide and TAPBPR.
source: Dissociation of FLPSDC*FPSV was only apparent in the first six hours in the presence of competitor peptide and TAPBPR (Figure 2A).
evidence: Demonstrated by fluorescence polarization measurements shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Dissociation of FLPSDC*FPSV from HLA-A2 was observed when a vast excess of unlabelled NLVPMVATV was used in the presence of TAPBPR.
source: Dissociation of FLPSDC*FPSV was also observed when a vast excess of unlabelled NLVPMVATV was used in the presence of TAPBPR (Figure 2B).
evidence: Demonstrated by fluorescence polarization measurements shown in Figure 2B.

claim: No enhancement in the dissociation of FLPSDC*FPSV was observed in the presence of TAPBPRTN5.
source: No enhancement in the dissociation of FLPSDC*FPSV was observed in the presence of TAPBPRTN5 (red line Figure 2B).
evidence: Demonstrated by fluorescence polarization measurements shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The ability of TAPBPR to enhance peptide dissociation is a direct consequence of TAPBPR binding to HLA-A2.
source: Thus the ability of TAPBPR to enhance peptide dissociation is a direct consequence of TAPBPR binding to HLA-A2.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of activity with TAPBPRTN5 mutant that cannot bind HLA-A2 (Figure 2B).

claim: TAPBPR catalysed binding of FLPSDC*FPSV to peptide-receptive HLA-A*02:01.
source: We found that TAPBPR catalysed binding of FLPSDC*FPSV to peptide-receptive HLA-A*02:01 (Figure 2C).
evidence: Demonstrated by fluorescence polarization measurements shown in Figure 2C.

claim: No enhancement in the association of FLPSDC*FPSV with HLA-A2 was observed in the presence of TAPBPRTN5.
source: In contrast, no enhancement in the association of FLPSDC*FPSV with HLA-A2 was observed in the presence of TAPBPRTN5 (Figure 2C), further demonstrating that a direct association between TAPBPR and HLA-A2 is required for TAPBPR to influence HLA-A2 peptide binding characteristics.
evidence: Demonstrated by fluorescence polarization measurements shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A direct association between TAPBPR and HLA-A2 is required for TAPBPR to influence HLA-A2 peptide binding characteristics.
source: In contrast, no enhancement in the association of FLPSDC*FPSV with HLA-A2 was observed in the presence of TAPBPRTN5 (Figure 2C), further demonstrating that a direct association between TAPBPR and HLA-A2 is required for TAPBPR to influence HLA-A2 peptide binding characteristics.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of activity with TAPBPRTN5 mutant that cannot bind HLA-A2 (Figure 2C).

claim: In the presence of TAPBPR, NLVPMVATV became a poorer competitor against FLPSDC*FPSV for binding to HLA-A*02:01.
source: In the presence of TAPBPR, NLVPMVATV became a poorer competitor (Figure 2D).
evidence: Demonstrated by peptide competition assays shown in Figure 2D.

claim: TAPBPRTN5 had no effect on peptide competition between NLVPMVATV and FLPSDC*FPSV.
source: TAPBPRTN5 had no effect on peptide competition (Figure 2D).
evidence: Demonstrated by peptide competition assays shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The dissociation rates of all tested peptides from HLA-A2 were enhanced in the presence of TAPBPR.
source: The dissociation rates of all peptides were enhanced in the presence of TAPBPR and in the presence of tapasin-jun as compared to competing peptide alone (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by fluorescence polarization measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The dissociation rates of all tested peptides from HLA-A2 were enhanced in the presence of tapasin-jun.
source: The dissociation rates of all peptides were enhanced in the presence of TAPBPR and in the presence of tapasin-jun as compared to competing peptide alone (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by fluorescence polarization measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: There are reproducible differences in the hierarchies of peptide dissociation between tapasin-jun and TAPBPR on HLA-A2.
source: This revealed reproducible differences in the hierarchies of peptide dissociation between tapasin-jun and TAPBPR on HLA-A2 (Figure 2E–G).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing relative half-lives of peptide dissociation over four independent experiments (Figure 2E–G).

claim: The half-life hierarchy for tapasin-mediated peptide dissociation was similar to the hierarchy observed in the absence of either cofactor.
source: Interestingly the half-life hierarchy for tapasin was similar to the hierarchy observed in the absence of either cofactor (competitor only) (Figure 2E,F), with the exception of the dissociation of GLDDIKDLK*V whose dissociation was relatively much slower in the presence of tapasin-jun compared to the other peptides than was observed in the presence of competitor only.
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing relative half-lives shown in Figure 2E and 2F.

claim: Tapasin enhancement of peptide dissociation generally parallels peptide-MHC complex stability.
source: This suggests that tapasin enhancement of peptide dissociation generally parallels peptide-MHC complex stability, as previously reported (Howarth et al., 2004).
evidence: Inferred from the similarity in dissociation hierarchies and supported by citation to published research.

claim: The half-life of peptides in the presence of TAPBPR does not follow the trend of paralleling peptide-MHC complex stability.
source: However, the half-life of peptides in the presence of TAPBPR does not follow this trend (Figure 2G).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing relative half-lives shown in Figure 2G with those in Figure 2E and 2F.

claim: TAPBPR enhanced dissociation of KLVK*EVIAV to a much smaller extent than was apparent in the presence of tapasin-jun or absence of either cofactor.
source: Specifically we observed that in comparison to the other peptides, TAPBPR enhanced dissociation of KLVK*EVIAV to a much smaller extent than was apparent in the presence of tapasin-jun or absence of either cofactor (competitor only) (Figure 2E–G).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing relative half-lives shown in Figure 2E–G.

claim: TAPBPR enhanced dissociation of FLPSDC*FPSV to a smaller extent than was apparent in the presence of tapasin-jun or absence of either cofactor.
source: The same was also true of FLPSDC*FPSV (Figure 2E–G).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing relative half-lives shown in Figure 2E–G.

claim: There are subtle differences in peptide specificity between tapasin and TAPBPR.
source: Taken together our results suggest firstly that both tapasin and TAPBPR enhance peptide dissociation, and secondly that there are subtle differences in regard to their peptide specificity.
evidence: Inferred from the different hierarchies of peptide dissociation observed for tapasin-jun and TAPBPR (Figure 2E–G).

claim: TAPBPR has a strong association with HLA-A2 and HLA-A68.
source: Immunoprecipitation of TAPBPR, followed by western blotting for MHC class I, confirmed the strong association between TAPBPR and the HLA-A allomorphs HLA-A2 and HLA-A68 (Figure 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoprecipitation and western blot analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: An association between TAPBPR and HLA-B allomorphs was detected, although weaker than with HLA-A2.
source: However, an association between TAPBPR and HLA-B allomorphs was also detected, although this was weaker (HLA-B8 and -B15), or below the limits of detection (HLA-B40), compared to that for HLA-A2 (Figure 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoprecipitation and western blot analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: TAPBPR interacts with a broader range of HLA molecules than originally appreciated.
source: Therefore, although there is clearly a strong association with those HLA-A allomorphs tested, TAPBPR interacts with a broader range of HLA molecules than originally appreciated (Boyle et al., 2013).
evidence: Inferred from the detection of interactions with HLA-B allomorphs in addition to HLA-A allomorphs (Figure 3).

claim: Dissociation of EIYK*RWIIL from HLA-B*08:01 was enhanced in the presence of TAPBPR.
source: We found that dissociation of EIYK*RWIIL was enhanced in the presence of TAPBPR (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by fluorescence polarization measurements shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: No enhancement of the dissociation of EIYK*RWIIL from HLA-B8:01-T134K was observed in the presence of TAPBPR.
source: No enhancement of the dissociation of EIYK*RWIIL was observed in the presence of TAPBPR using HLA-B8:01-T134K in which the T134 residue had been mutated to lysine, which abrogates binding of TAPBPR to MHC I (Hermann et al., 2013) (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), demonstrating that the enhanced peptide dissociation was dependent on a direct interaction between TAPBPR and HLA-B8.
evidence: Demonstrated by fluorescence polarization measurements shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The T134K mutation in HLA-B8:01 abrogates binding of TAPBPR to MHC I.
source: No enhancement of the dissociation of EIYK*RWIIL was observed in the presence of TAPBPR using HLA-B8:01-T134K in which the T134 residue had been mutated to lysine, which abrogates binding of TAPBPR to MHC I (Hermann et al., 2013) (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), demonstrating that the enhanced peptide dissociation was dependent on a direct interaction between TAPBPR and HLA-B8.
evidence: Supported by citation to published research and confirmed by lack of functional activity (Figure 4B).

claim: The enhanced peptide dissociation from HLA-B8 was dependent on a direct interaction between TAPBPR and HLA-B8.
source: No enhancement of the dissociation of EIYK*RWIIL was observed in the presence of TAPBPR using HLA-B8:01-T134K in which the T134 residue had been mutated to lysine, which abrogates binding of TAPBPR to MHC I (Hermann et al., 2013) (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), demonstrating that the enhanced peptide dissociation was dependent on a direct interaction between TAPBPR and HLA-B8.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of activity with T134K mutant that cannot bind TAPBPR (Figure 4B).

claim: The dissociation of ELRSRK*WAI from HLA-B*08:01 was not altered in the presence of TAPBPR.
source: The dissociation of ELRSRK*WAI was not altered in the presence of TAPBPR (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C) and only a very slight change in dissociation of FLRGRK*YGL was observed in the presence of TAPBPR (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Demonstrated by fluorescence polarization measurements shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Only a very slight change in dissociation of FLRGRK*YGL from HLA-B*08:01 was observed in the presence of TAPBPR.
source: The dissociation of ELRSRK*WAI was not altered in the presence of TAPBPR (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C) and only a very slight change in dissociation of FLRGRK*YGL was observed in the presence of TAPBPR (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Demonstrated by fluorescence polarization measurements shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: TAPBPR can enhance peptide dissociation from HLA-B8 in a peptide specific manner.
source: Therefore, our results suggest that TAPBPR can enhance peptide dissociation from HLA-B8 but that this effect is peptide specific.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects on dissociation of different peptides (Figures 4A-D).

claim: Tapasin exhibits peptide specificity in regard to peptide dissociation.
source: Tapasin has also been reported to exhibit peptide specificity in regard to peptide dissociation (Chen and Bouvier, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research.

claim: Tapasin-jun accelerated dissociation of FITC labelled EIYK*RWIIL and FLRGRK*YGL from HLA-B*08:01fos.
source: Like TAPBPR, tapasin-jun accelerated dissociation of fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC) labelled versions of both EIYK*RWIIL and FLRGRK*YGL from HLA-B*08:01fos, while the dissociation of ELRSRK*WAI was insensitive to tapasin-jun (Chen and Bouvier, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research.

claim: The dissociation of ELRSRK*WAI from HLA-B*08:01fos was insensitive to tapasin-jun.
source: Like TAPBPR, tapasin-jun accelerated dissociation of fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC) labelled versions of both EIYK*RWIIL and FLRGRK*YGL from HLA-B*08:01fos, while the dissociation of ELRSRK*WAI was insensitive to tapasin-jun (Chen and Bouvier, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research.

claim: TAPBPR enhanced binding of EIYK*RWIIL to peptide-receptive HLA-B*08:01fos molecules.
source: As with HLA-A2, we observed that TAPBPR could enhance peptide binding to peptide-receptive HLA-B*08:01fos molecules. However, this was only observed with EIYK*RWIIL (Figure 4E) and the binding of ELRSRK*WAI or FLRGRK*YGL to peptide receptive HLA-B*08:01fos was not altered in the presence of TAPBPR (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: Demonstrated by fluorescence polarization measurements shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The binding of ELRSRK*WAI to peptide receptive HLA-B*08:01fos was not altered in the presence of TAPBPR.
source: As with HLA-A2, we observed that TAPBPR could enhance peptide binding to peptide-receptive HLA-B*08:01fos molecules. However, this was only observed with EIYK*RWIIL (Figure 4E) and the binding of ELRSRK*WAI or FLRGRK*YGL to peptide receptive HLA-B*08:01fos was not altered in the presence of TAPBPR (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: Demonstrated by fluorescence polarization measurements shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The binding of FLRGRK*YGL to peptide receptive HLA-B*08:01fos was not altered in the presence of TAPBPR.
source: As with HLA-A2, we observed that TAPBPR could enhance peptide binding to peptide-receptive HLA-B*08:01fos molecules. However, this was only observed with EIYK*RWIIL (Figure 4E) and the binding of ELRSRK*WAI or FLRGRK*YGL to peptide receptive HLA-B*08:01fos was not altered in the presence of TAPBPR (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: Demonstrated by fluorescence polarization measurements shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Tapasin-jun enhanced binding of FITC labelled ELRSRK*WAI and FLRGRK*YGL to peptide-receptive HLA-B*08:01fos molecules.
source: This contrasts with the results previously published by Chen and Bouvier, who observed that tapasin-jun enhanced binding of FITC labelled versions of ELRSRK*WAI and FLRGRK*YGL to peptide-receptive HLA-B*08:01fos molecules (Chen and Bouvier, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research.

claim: TAPBPR can enhance the loading of peptide onto HLA-B*08:01 in a peptide specific manner.
source: Taken together the data indicate that TAPBPR can enhance the loading of peptide onto HLA-B*08:01, and that this is peptide specific.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects on binding of different peptides (Figures 4E-G).

claim: There are differences in peptide specificity between tapasin and TAPBPR with respect to HLA-B*08:01 peptide-loading.
source: Furthermore, there are differences in peptide specificity between tapasin and TAPBPR with respect to HLA-B*08:01 peptide-loading.
evidence: Inferred from the different peptide-specific effects observed for TAPBPR compared to published results for tapasin-jun.

claim: TAPBPR increased peptide exchange on HLA-B*08:01 by making the low affinity peptide EIYKRWIIL a poorer competitor against the high affinity labelled peptide ELRSRK*WAI.
source: Finally we showed that, like tapasin (Chen and Bouvier, 2007), TAPBPR increased peptide exchange on HLA-B*08:01 since the low affinity peptide EIYKRWIIL became a poorer competitor against the high affinity labelled peptide ELRSRK*WAI in the presence of TAPBPR (Figure 4H).
evidence: Demonstrated by peptide competition assays shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Upon treatment with IFN-γ, TAPBPR expression was induced in HeLa, but not in the HeLa-TAPBPR KO line.
source: We found that upon treatment with IFN-γ, TAPBPR expression was induced in HeLa, but not in the HeLa-TAPBPR KO line (Figure 5A).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Tapasin expression was not affected by the sgRNA targeted to TAPBPR.
source: Tapasin expression was not affected by the sgRNA targeted to TAPBPR (Figure 5A).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In the absence of TAPBPR, cell surface expression of MHC class I in IFN-γ treated HeLa did not significantly change.
source: In the absence of TAPBPR, cell surface expression of MHC class I in IFN-γ treated HeLa did not significantly change as determined by W6/32 staining and flow cytometry (Figure 5B).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In IFN-γ treated HeLa cells, 1607 different peptides were isolated on MHC class I, compared with 2074 in IFN-γ treated HeLa-TAPBPR KO cells.
source: In IFN-γ treated HeLa cells, we isolated 1607 different peptides on MHC class I, compared with 2074 in IFN-γ treated HeLa-TAPBPR KO cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: Determined by mass spectrometry analysis of eluted peptides as shown in Figure 5C.

claim: 1398 peptides were shared between IFN-γ treated HeLa and HeLa-TAPBPR KO cells, but 209 peptides were unique to HeLa and 676 were unique to HeLa-TAPBPR KO.
source: 1398 peptides were shared between the two cell lines, but 209 peptides were unique to HeLa and 676 were unique to HeLa-TAPBPR KO (Figure 5C).
evidence: Determined by mass spectrometry analysis of eluted peptides as shown in Figure 5C.

claim: An increased peptide repertoire was observed for both HLA-A*68:02 and HLA-B*15:03 in the absence of TAPBPR.
source: When the peptides were subdivided into those predicted to bind to HLA-A*68:02 or HLA-B*15:03 based on anchor sequences, an increased repertoire was observed for both allomorphs in the absence of TAPBPR (Figure 5C).
evidence: Determined by mass spectrometry analysis and NetMHC prediction as shown in Figure 5C.

claim: A similar pattern of increased peptide diversity was observed in IFN-γ treated HeLa-S cells upon TAPBPR depletion using shRNA to TAPBPR.
source: Consistent with these findings, a similar pattern of increased peptide diversity was also observed in IFN-γ treated HeLa-S cells upon TAPBPR depletion using shRNA to TAPBPR (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Determined by mass spectrometry analysis as shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The total number of different peptides isolated from MHC class I was decreased in cells over-expressing TAPBPR, from 819 MHC class I restricted peptides from HeLa cells down to 296 MHC class I restricted peptides isolated from HeLa cells over-expressing TAPBPR.
source: We found the total number of different peptides isolated from MHC class I was decreased in cells over-expressing TAPBPR, from 819 MHC class I restricted peptides from HeLa cells down to 296 MHC class I restricted peptides isolated from HeLa cells over-expressing TAPBPR.
evidence: Determined by mass spectrometry analysis of eluted peptides as shown in Figure 5D.

claim: 210 peptides were shared between HeLa and HeLa cells over-expressing TAPBPR.
source: 210 peptides were shared between the two cell lines (Figure 5D).
evidence: Determined by mass spectrometry analysis of eluted peptides as shown in Figure 5D.

claim: There was an enhancement of canonical anchor residues in the peptides eluted from TAPBPR expressing cells.
source: We found there was an enhancement of canonical anchor residues in the peptides eluted from TAPBPR expressing cells (Figure 5E–H).
evidence: Demonstrated by analysis of P2 and C-terminal anchor residues shown in Figure 5E–H.

claim: In IFN-γ treated HeLa cells, 53% of the shared peptides predicted to be bound to HLA-A*A68:02 had classic anchor residues compared to 43% of the peptides found exclusively in TAPBPR deficient cells.
source: For example, in IFN-γ treated HeLa cells 53% of the shared peptides predicted to be bound to HLA-A*A68:02 (which had presumably been subjected to TAPBPR function) had classic anchor residues (P2 = threonine or valine, PΩ = valine or leucine) compared to 43% of the peptides found exclusively in TAPBPR deficient cells which are the peptides that TAPBPR usually restricts (Figure 5E).
evidence: Determined by analysis of anchor residues shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Only 5% of the peptides eluted exclusively from TAPBPR deficient cells predicted to bind HLA-B*15:03 contained classical anchor motifs compared to 24% of the peptides eluted from TAPBPR over expressing cells.
source: More striking was the restriction of peptides predicted to be bound by HLA-B*15:03 in cells over-expressing TAPBPR (Figure 5H) with only 5% of the peptides eluted exclusively from TAPBPR deficient cells (i.e. the TAPBPR restricted peptides) containing classical anchor motifs (P2 = glutamine or lysine, PΩ = tyrosine or phenylalanine) compared to 24% of the peptides eluted from TAPBPR over expressing cells (i.e. the TAPBPR permitted peptides).
evidence: Determined by analysis of anchor residues shown in Figure 5H.

claim: TAPBPR restriction in vivo helps to remove some peptides of lower affinity and assists in improving peptide selection on MHC class I.
source: This suggests TAPBPR restriction in vivo helps to remove some peptides of lower affinity and therefore assists in improving peptide selection on MHC class I.
evidence: Inferred from the enhancement of canonical anchor residues in TAPBPR-permitted peptides (Figure 5E–H).

claim: TAPBPR expression did not have a dramatic effect on peptide length.
source: We found TAPBPR expression did not have a dramatic effect on peptide length (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by analysis of peptide length shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Surface expression of HLA-A2 was similar in IFN-γ treated wild-type, TAPBPR depleted and tapasin deficient KBM-7 cells.
source: Surface expression of HLA-A2 was similar in IFN-γ treated wild-type (WT), TAPBPR depleted and tapasin deficient KBM-7 cells (Figure 6A).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: TAPBPR depletion resulted in increased peptide diversity on HLA-A2 in KBM-7 cells.
source: While TAPBPR depletion resulted in increased peptide diversity on HLA-A2 (Figure 6B), tapasin deficiency did not significantly change the total number of peptides presented on HLA-A2 (Figure 6B), although the peptide repertoire was significantly different between IFN-γ treated WT and tapasin deficient KBM-7 cells (Figure 6C).
evidence: Determined by mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Tapasin deficiency did not significantly change the total number of peptides presented on HLA-A2 in KBM-7 cells.
source: While TAPBPR depletion resulted in increased peptide diversity on HLA-A2 (Figure 6B), tapasin deficiency did not significantly change the total number of peptides presented on HLA-A2 (Figure 6B), although the peptide repertoire was significantly different between IFN-γ treated WT and tapasin deficient KBM-7 cells (Figure 6C).
evidence: Determined by mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The peptide repertoire was significantly different between IFN-γ treated WT and tapasin deficient KBM-7 cells.
source: While TAPBPR depletion resulted in increased peptide diversity on HLA-A2 (Figure 6B), tapasin deficiency did not significantly change the total number of peptides presented on HLA-A2 (Figure 6B), although the peptide repertoire was significantly different between IFN-γ treated WT and tapasin deficient KBM-7 cells (Figure 6C).
evidence: Demonstrated by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Surface expression of HLA-B40 was similar in IFN-γ treated WT and TAPBPR depleted KBM-7 cells, but was reduced in tapasin deficient KBM-7 cells.
source: Surface expression of HLA-B40 was similar in IFN-γ treated WT and TAPBPR depleted cells, but was reduced in tapasin deficient KBM-7 cells (Figure 6D).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: TAPBPR depletion increased peptide diversity on HLA-B40 and -C03 in IFN-γ treated KBM-7 cells.
source: TAPBPR depletion and tapasin deficiency produced different effects on peptides presented by HLA-B40 and -C03 in IFN-γ treated KBM-7 cells, with TAPBPR depletion increasing peptide diversity and tapasin deficiency decreasing the number of peptides presented (Figure 6E,F).
evidence: Determined by mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 6E,F.

claim: Tapasin deficiency decreased the number of peptides presented on HLA-B40 and -C03 in IFN-γ treated KBM-7 cells.
source: TAPBPR depletion and tapasin deficiency produced different effects on peptides presented by HLA-B40 and -C03 in IFN-γ treated KBM-7 cells, with TAPBPR depletion increasing peptide diversity and tapasin deficiency decreasing the number of peptides presented (Figure 6E,F).
evidence: Determined by mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 6E,F.

claim: Tapasin deficiency decreases peptide number for mouse MHC I molecules H-2Db and Kb.
source: A similar effect of tapasin deficiency decreasing peptide number has recently been reported for the mouse MHC I molecule H-2Db and Kb (Kanaseki et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research.

claim: Within the cellular environment, tapasin and TAPBPR shape the peptide repertoire in distinct ways.
source: Therefore, although in vitro TAPBPR and tapasin both function as peptide exchange catalysts, within the cellular environment the two molecules shape the peptide repertoire in distinct ways.
evidence: Inferred from the different effects on peptide repertoire observed for TAPBPR depletion versus tapasin deficiency (Figure 6).

claim: There was a >90% reduction in the amount of HLA-A2 bound to TAPBPR following the addition of the NLVPMVATV peptide.
source: Western blot analysis of the proteins co-immunoprecipitated with TAPBPR revealed a >90% reduction in the amount of HLA-A2 bound to TAPBPR following the addition of the NLVPMVATV peptide (Figure 7).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Less dissociation of HLA-A2 from TAPBPR was observed using NAVPMVATV (Δ2) and NLVPMVATM (Δ9) peptides, in which one anchor residue had been substituted.
source: Less dissociation of HLA-A2 from TAPBPR was observed using NAVPMVATV (Δ2) and NLVPMVATM (Δ9) peptides, in which one anchor residue had been substituted, while the NAVPMVATM (Δ2/9) peptide, in which both anchor residues were substituted was unable to induce any HLA-A2 dissociation (Figure 7).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: The NAVPMVATM (Δ2/9) peptide, in which both anchor residues were substituted, was unable to induce any HLA-A2 dissociation from TAPBPR.
source: Less dissociation of HLA-A2 from TAPBPR was observed using NAVPMVATV (Δ2) and NLVPMVATM (Δ9) peptides, in which one anchor residue had been substituted, while the NAVPMVATM (Δ2/9) peptide, in which both anchor residues were substituted was unable to induce any HLA-A2 dissociation (Figure 7).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Peptide loaded HLA-A2 was released from TAPBPR upon incubation with the NLVPMVATV peptide but not in the absence of the peptide.
source: Peptide loaded HLA-A2 was released from TAPBPR upon incubation with the NLVPMVATV peptide but not in the absence of the peptide (lanes 2 and 1 respectively Figure 7).
evidence: Demonstrated by re-immunoprecipitation and western blot analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Only trace amounts of peptide loaded HLA-A2:β2m molecules were released from TAPBPR using the Δ2 and Δ9 peptides.
source: Only trace amounts of peptide loaded HLA-A2:β2m molecules were released from TAPBPR using the Δ2 and Δ9 peptides (lane 3 and 4, Figure 7), while no peptide loaded HLA-A2 was released from TAPBPR using the Δ2/9 peptide (lane 5 Figure 7).
evidence: Demonstrated by re-immunoprecipitation and western blot analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: No peptide loaded HLA-A2 was released from TAPBPR using the Δ2/9 peptide.
source: Only trace amounts of peptide loaded HLA-A2:β2m molecules were released from TAPBPR using the Δ2 and Δ9 peptides (lane 3 and 4, Figure 7), while no peptide loaded HLA-A2 was released from TAPBPR using the Δ2/9 peptide (lane 5 Figure 7).
evidence: Demonstrated by re-immunoprecipitation and western blot analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: MHC I molecules bound to TAPBPR are in a peptide-receptive state.
source: Together these results demonstrate that MHC I molecules bound to TAPBPR are in a peptide-receptive state and that the association between TAPBPR and MHC I is reduced by high affinity peptide resulting in peptide loaded MHC I being released from TAPBPR.
evidence: Demonstrated by peptide-induced release of MHC I from TAPBPR (Figure 7).

claim: The association between TAPBPR and MHC I is reduced by high affinity peptide resulting in peptide loaded MHC I being released from TAPBPR.
source: Together these results demonstrate that MHC I molecules bound to TAPBPR are in a peptide-receptive state and that the association between TAPBPR and MHC I is reduced by high affinity peptide resulting in peptide loaded MHC I being released from TAPBPR.
evidence: Demonstrated by peptide-induced release of MHC I from TAPBPR (Figure 7).

claim: Surface expression of HLA-A2 is relatively unaffected in the absence of tapasin.
source: Previous studies have reported that, although the quantity of naturally processed peptides stably bound by HLA-A*02:01 is significantly reduced in the absence of tapasin (Barber et al., 2001), surface expression of HLA-A2 is relatively unaffected in the absence of tapasin (Greenwood et al., 1994; Barber et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research.

claim: The quantity of naturally processed peptides stably bound by HLA-A*02:01 is significantly reduced in the absence of tapasin.
source: Previous studies have reported that, although the quantity of naturally processed peptides stably bound by HLA-A*02:01 is significantly reduced in the absence of tapasin (Barber et al., 2001), surface expression of HLA-A2 is relatively unaffected in the absence of tapasin (Greenwood et al., 1994; Barber et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research.

claim: HLA-B7 expression is reduced in the absence of tapasin.
source: In contrast, HLA-B7 expression is reduced in the absence of tapasin (Rizvi et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research.

claim: There was an increased interaction between HLA-A2 and TAPBPR in the absence of tapasin in the 721 cell line series.
source: Consistent with our previous findings in tapasin deficient KBM-7 cells (Hermann et al., 2013), we found an increased interaction between HLA-A2 and TAPBPR in the absence of tapasin in the 721 cell line series (compare TAPBPR IP lanes 1 and 3, Figure 8A) which was apparent even though the expression of TAPBPR appeared to be slightly higher in .220 cells compared to .221 cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoprecipitation and western blot analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: There was an increased interaction between HLA-B7 and TAPBPR in the absence of tapasin.
source: This phenomenon does not appear to be restricted to HLA-A2, as we similarly observed an increased interaction between HLA-B7 and TAPBPR in the absence of tapasin (compare TAPBPR IP lanes 1 and 3, Figure 8A).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoprecipitation and western blot analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The steady state level of both HLA-B7 and HLA-A2 is severely reduced in the absence of tapasin.
source: The increased association between TAPBPR and MHC class I occurs despite the fact that the steady state level of both HLA-B7 and HLA-A2 is severely reduced in the absence of tapasin (compare lysate lanes 1 and 3, Figure 8A).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot analysis of lysates shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The steady state level of HLA-A2 at the cell surface was not affected by TAPBPR depletion in tapasin sufficient cells.
source: We found that the steady state level of HLA-A2 at the cell surface was not affected by TAPBPR depletion in tapasin sufficient cells (left panel Figure 8B).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The depletion of TAPBPR in tapasin negative cells resulted in a ∼75% decrease in cell surface expression of HLA-A2.
source: However, the depletion of TAPBPR in tapasin negative cells resulted in a ∼75% decrease in cell surface expression of HLA-A2 (right panel Figure 8B).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claim: A significant decrease in the surface expression of HLA-B7 was observed upon depletion of TAPBPR, even in the presence of tapasin.
source: In contrast, using an antibody to the Bw6 epitope we observed a significant decrease in the surface expression of HLA-B7 upon depletion of TAPBPR, even in the presence of tapasin (left panel Figure 8C).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Only residual expression of HLA-B7 was observed upon the depletion of TAPBPR in the tapasin negative cell 721.220.
source: Only residual expression of HLA-B7 was observed upon the depletion of TAPBPR in the tapasin negative cell 721.220 (right panel Figure 8C).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 8C.

claim: HLA allomorphs differ in their dependency on TAPBPR.
source: These results suggest that HLA allomorphs differ in their dependency on TAPBPR, and that tapasin and TAPBPR work together to optimise surface expression of MHC class I molecules.
evidence: Inferred from the different effects of TAPBPR depletion on HLA-A2 versus HLA-B7 surface expression (Figure 8B,C).

claim: Tapasin and TAPBPR work together to optimise surface expression of MHC class I molecules.
source: These results suggest that HLA allomorphs differ in their dependency on TAPBPR, and that tapasin and TAPBPR work together to optimise surface expression of MHC class I molecules.
evidence: Inferred from the cumulative effects of tapasin deficiency and TAPBPR depletion on MHC class I surface expression (Figure 8B,C).

claim: The thermal stability of HLA-A2 was reduced in TAPBPR depleted cells.
source: We found that the thermal stability of HLA-A2 was reduced in TAPBPR depleted cells (compare grey bar with the red bar in Figure 8D).
evidence: Demonstrated by thermal stability assays shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The thermal stability of MHC class I correlates with the affinity of its peptide cargo.
source: As the thermal stability of MHC class I correlates with the affinity of its peptide cargo (Williams et al., 2002), these results support the hypothesis that TAPBPR assists in the selection of stable peptides on MHC class I molecules.
evidence: Supported by citation to published research.

claim: TAPBPR assists in the selection of stable peptides on MHC class I molecules.
source: As the thermal stability of MHC class I correlates with the affinity of its peptide cargo (Williams et al., 2002), these results support the hypothesis that TAPBPR assists in the selection of stable peptides on MHC class I molecules.
evidence: Inferred from the reduced thermal stability of HLA-A2 in TAPBPR depleted cells (Figure 8D).

claim: The effect of TAPBPR depletion on HLA-A2 thermal stability was not as severe as that observed in the absence of tapasin.
source: However, the effect of TAPBPR depletion on HLA-A2 thermal stability was not as severe as that observed in the absence of tapasin (compared red and blue bars in Figure 8B).
evidence: Demonstrated by thermal stability assays shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The thermal stability of peptide loaded HLA-A2 was further decreased when TAPBPR was depleted in tapasin negative cells.
source: The thermal stability of peptide loaded HLA-A2 was further decreased when TAPBPR was depleted in tapasin negative cells (green bar in Figure 8B).
evidence: Demonstrated by thermal stability assays shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Both HLA-A2 and –B7 exhibited faster decay rates from the cell surface in TAPBPR-depleted cells.
source: Both HLA-A2 and –B7 exhibited faster decay rates from the cell surface in TAPBPR-depleted cells (Figure 8E‚F), suggesting that in the absence of TAPBPR MHC class I molecules containing lower affinity peptides can escape to the cell surface.
evidence: Demonstrated by brefeldin A decay assays shown in Figure 8E,F.

claim: In the absence of TAPBPR, MHC class I molecules containing lower affinity peptides can escape to the cell surface.
source: Both HLA-A2 and –B7 exhibited faster decay rates from the cell surface in TAPBPR-depleted cells (Figure 8E‚F), suggesting that in the absence of TAPBPR MHC class I molecules containing lower affinity peptides can escape to the cell surface.
evidence: Inferred from the faster decay rates observed in TAPBPR-depleted cells (Figure 8E,F).

claim: For HLA-A2, tapasin deficiency had a more severe effect than TAPBPR depletion on the rate of decay from the cell surface.
source: For HLA-A2, tapasin deficiency had a more severe effect than TAPBPR depletion on the rate of decay (compare the blue line with the red line in Figure 8E) while for HLA-B7, tapasin deficiency and TAPBPR depletion had a similar effect on the decay rate (see the overlap of the blue and red line in Figure 8F).
evidence: Demonstrated by brefeldin A decay assays shown in Figure 8E.

claim: For HLA-B7, tapasin deficiency and TAPBPR depletion had a similar effect on the decay rate from the cell surface.
source: For HLA-A2, tapasin deficiency had a more severe effect than TAPBPR depletion on the rate of decay (compare the blue line with the red line in Figure 8E) while for HLA-B7, tapasin deficiency and TAPBPR depletion had a similar effect on the decay rate (see the overlap of the blue and red line in Figure 8F).
evidence: Demonstrated by brefeldin A decay assays shown in Figure 8F.

claim: For both HLA-A2 and –B7, the loss of both tapasin and TAPBPR had an accumulative effect on MHC class I stability.
source: For both HLA-A2 and –B7 the loss of both tapasin and TAPBPR had an accumulative effect on MHC class I stability (see green line in Figure 8E,F).
evidence: Demonstrated by brefeldin A decay assays shown in Figure 8E,F.

claim: TAPBPR has a role in the selection of stable peptides for MHC class I molecules in vivo.
source: Together, these results clearly demonstrate a role for TAPBPR in the selection of stable peptides for MHC class I molecules in vivo and support the hypothesis that TAPBPR can enhance peptide optimisation in the absence of tapasin.
evidence: Demonstrated by thermal stability and decay rate experiments (Figure 8D-F).

claim: TAPBPR can enhance peptide optimisation in the absence of tapasin.
source: Together, these results clearly demonstrate a role for TAPBPR in the selection of stable peptides for MHC class I molecules in vivo and support the hypothesis that TAPBPR can enhance peptide optimisation in the absence of tapasin.
evidence: Inferred from the effects of TAPBPR depletion in tapasin-deficient cells (Figure 8).

claim: The PLC is considered to be the major site where MHC class I molecules are loaded with high affinity peptides.
source: The PLC is considered to be the major site where MHC class I molecules are loaded with high affinity peptides, with the tapasin-ERp57 conjugate described as the functional unit (Momburg and Tan, 2002; Williams et al., 2002; Howarth et al., 2004; Wearsch and Cresswell, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research.

claim: The tapasin-ERp57 conjugate is described as the functional unit of the PLC.
source: The PLC is considered to be the major site where MHC class I molecules are loaded with high affinity peptides, with the tapasin-ERp57 conjugate described as the functional unit (Momburg and Tan, 2002; Williams et al., 2002; Howarth et al., 2004; Wearsch and Cresswell, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research.

claim: The luminal domains of TAPBPR alone have sufficient affinity for MHC class I to promote peptide loading and to catalyse peptide exchange.
source: This suggests that the luminal region of TAPBPR alone has sufficient affinity for MHC class I to promote peptide loading and to catalyse peptide exchange and does not require other co-factors or to be artificially tethered to MHC class I to perform this function.
evidence: Inferred from the functional activity of soluble TAPBPR in vitro without artificial tethering (Figures 2, 4).

claim: Soluble tapasin does not associate productively with MHC class I in vitro alone.
source: This is in contrast to soluble tapasin, which others have found does not associate productively with MHC class I in vitro alone, and instead requires either conjugation to ERp57 or to be artificially tethered to MHC class I (Chen and Bouvier, 2007; Wearsch and Cresswell, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research.

claim: TAPBPR has a higher affinity for MHC class I than tapasin.
source: We speculate the difference in affinity of tapasin and TAPBPR for MHC class I may have evolved as a consequence of the distinct cellular environment the two peptide exchange catalysts function: tapasin functioning in the context of the PLC, where other proteins collectively form a mutually supportive interaction scaffold, and TAPBPR functioning outside the confines of the PLC.
evidence: Inferred from the ability of TAPBPR to function without artificial tethering while tapasin requires it, and from the different cellular locations of function.

claim: Tapasin functions in the context of the PLC, where other proteins collectively form a mutually supportive interaction scaffold.
source: We speculate the difference in affinity of tapasin and TAPBPR for MHC class I may have evolved as a consequence of the distinct cellular environment the two peptide exchange catalysts function: tapasin functioning in the context of the PLC, where other proteins collectively form a mutually supportive interaction scaffold, and TAPBPR functioning outside the confines of the PLC.
evidence: This is established knowledge about tapasin function.

claim: TAPBPR functions outside the confines of the PLC.
source: We speculate the difference in affinity of tapasin and TAPBPR for MHC class I may have evolved as a consequence of the distinct cellular environment the two peptide exchange catalysts function: tapasin functioning in the context of the PLC, where other proteins collectively form a mutually supportive interaction scaffold, and TAPBPR functioning outside the confines of the PLC.
evidence: Supported by previous findings that TAPBPR is not an integral component of the PLC.

claim: Tapasin and TAPBPR work together in a sequential manner.
source: Clearly, a new picture concerning how peptides are selected for presentation by MHC class I molecules is emerging. Our findings are consistent with tapasin and TAPBPR working together in a sequential manner (Figure 9).
evidence: Inferred from the combined effects of tapasin and TAPBPR on peptide selection and MHC class I stability.

claim: The initial peptide loading of MHC I molecules is likely to occur within the PLC and to be assisted by tapasin.
source: The initial peptide loading of MHC I molecules is likely to occur within the PLC and to be assisted by tapasin.
evidence: This is established knowledge about tapasin function in the PLC.

claim: Outside of the PLC, the stability of peptide:MHC I complexes is monitored by TAPBPR.
source: We propose that outside of the PLC, the stability of peptide:MHC I complexes is monitored by TAPBPR.
evidence: Inferred from the peptide exchange activity of TAPBPR and its function outside the PLC.

claim: MHC class I molecules loaded with high affinity peptides will either circumvent TAPBPR-mediated peptide editing completely or pass through this quality control checkpoint.
source: Those molecules loaded with high affinity peptides will either circumvent TAPBPR-mediated peptide editing completely or pass through this quality control checkpoint.
evidence: Inferred from the peptide-induced release of MHC I from TAPBPR (Figure 7) and the restriction of lower affinity peptides.

claim: For MHC class I molecules loaded with peptides of intermediate or low affinity, TAPBPR-mediated peptide editing proceeds.
source: For MHC class I molecules loaded with peptides of intermediate or low affinity, TAPBPR-mediated peptide editing proceeds.
evidence: Inferred from the peptide exchange activity of TAPBPR and the increased diversity of peptides in TAPBPR-deficient cells.

claim: The relatively peptide-rich environment of the PLC may allow tapasin to promote peptide binding and produce a relatively broad peptide repertoire.
source: The relatively peptide-rich environment of the PLC may allow tapasin to promote peptide binding and produce a relatively broad peptide repertoire.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the known function of tapasin in the PLC.

claim: As an MHC I molecule moves away from the PLC, the gradient of optimal peptides is likely to decrease.
source: However, presumably as an MHC I molecule moves away from the PLC, the gradient of optimal peptides is likely to decrease and therefore TAPBPR-mediated peptide editing events within such an environment may favour peptide dissociation rather than association.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the peptide environment outside the PLC.

claim: TAPBPR-mediated peptide editing events in a peptide-poor environment may favour peptide dissociation rather than association.
source: However, presumably as an MHC I molecule moves away from the PLC, the gradient of optimal peptides is likely to decrease and therefore TAPBPR-mediated peptide editing events within such an environment may favour peptide dissociation rather than association.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the peptide environment and observed increased peptide diversity in TAPBPR-deficient cells.

claim: In a peptide rich environment, acceleration of both association and dissociation by tapasin contributes to editing.
source: Thus we speculate that, in a peptide rich environment, acceleration of both association and dissociation (by tapasin) contributes to editing; while in a peptide dilute environment, acceleration of dissociation only (by TAPBPR) may dominate editing, consistent with the increased peptide repertoire observed in TAPBPR deficient cells.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the different effects of tapasin and TAPBPR on peptide repertoire.

claim: In a peptide dilute environment, acceleration of dissociation only by TAPBPR may dominate editing.
source: Thus we speculate that, in a peptide rich environment, acceleration of both association and dissociation (by tapasin) contributes to editing; while in a peptide dilute environment, acceleration of dissociation only (by TAPBPR) may dominate editing, consistent with the increased peptide repertoire observed in TAPBPR deficient cells.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the increased peptide diversity in TAPBPR-deficient cells.

claim: TAPBPR may restrict peptide presentation by enhancing the selection of high affinity peptide on MHC class I.
source: Thus, TAPBPR may restrict peptide presentation by enhancing the selection of high affinity peptide on MHC class I.
evidence: Inferred from the increased peptide diversity in TAPBPR-deficient cells and the enhancement of canonical anchor residues in TAPBPR-permitted peptides.
